items.title: Star performers always come back down — not because of psychology
items.claim: A rookie has a breakout season. The next year, his performance drops. Headlines say 'sophomore slump' and 'pressure of expectations'. A statistician would have predicted the drop without ever watching a game.

options.text: Extreme observations have a luck component; the next observation typically regresses toward the underlying mean. The 'rookie season' was partially luck; the next season's mean performance reflects underlying skill, with less luck

items.reveal_title: Galton, sons of tall fathers, and luck
items.reveal:
Francis Galton (1886) measured heights of fathers and sons. He noticed: tall fathers tend to have shorter sons, and short fathers tend to have taller sons. Not because fathers' height 'reverts' to a population mean, but because extreme parental heights are partly random (chance of which alleles were inherited from grandparents).

Galton called this 'regression to mediocrity', later 'regression to the mean'. The term 'regression analysis' for fitting lines to data descends from this observation.

General principle: if a measurement combines skill (or any persistent factor) and chance, extreme measurements come from combinations of GOOD skill AND GOOD luck. Replicate the measurement, and on average the luck component will be average — so the second measurement regresses toward the underlying skill mean.

Applications:
- Sports: 'sophomore slump' is regression, not psychology.
- Medicine: patients with extreme symptoms tend to improve at the next visit (regression to a less-extreme baseline). Many treatments look effective in uncontrolled trials simply because of regression.
- Education: 'praise reduces performance, criticism improves it' (Kahneman's famous Israeli pilot training observation) — actually regression after extreme performances followed by interventions.
- Finance: top-performing fund managers tend to revert toward average; investors who chase last year's winners underperform.

Correct analysis requires CONTROL groups or careful baseline modelling. Without them, regression masquerades as 'real' effects.
items.why: Performance fluctuations get psychological explanations they don't need. The math of extreme values guarantees that record-breakers tend to come back down. Understanding regression to the mean dissolves many spurious 'effects'.

items.title: A university that favoured women overall was sued for discriminating against them
items.claim: Berkeley's graduate admissions, 1973: men admitted at 44%, women at 35%. Looks like discrimination. Break it down by department — and in most departments, women were admitted at HIGHER rates. The overall trend reverses when disaggregated.
items.prompt: How can the parts and the whole point opposite ways?

options.text: Simpson's paradox: women applied disproportionately to highly competitive departments with low admission rates for everyone; the overall ratio is dominated by where applicants applied, not how each department treated them
Only one of the figures is true

items.reveal_title: Simpson's paradox in real admissions data
items.reveal:
Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell (Science 1975) analysed Berkeley's 1973 fall admissions. Aggregate: 44% of male applicants admitted vs 35% of female. Looks like a 9-point bias.

Department-by-department: of the 6 largest departments, 4 actually favoured women (higher admission rate). Only 2 favoured men.

What's going on: women disproportionately applied to humanities and social sciences (low admission rates for everyone, ~5-30%). Men disproportionately applied to physics, engineering, etc. (higher admission rates, ~50-70%). The aggregate bias against women was driven by their CHOICE of department, not by departmental policies.

The pattern is named after Edward H. Simpson (1951 statistician), though Pearson and Yule had noted it earlier.

The lesson: aggregating data across groups can REVERSE the direction of a trend present in every group. Whenever you see a aggregate correlation in observational data, ask whether breaking it down by relevant subgroup changes the story.

Real-world examples: kidney stone treatment effectiveness, racial sentencing disparities, COVID death rates by age, batting averages across seasons.
items.why: Aggregate statistics feel definitive. Disaggregating by a confounder can reverse the apparent trend — sometimes drastically. The same data tell different stories at different levels.

items.title: Most people earn less than the average wage
items.claim: If you tell people the 'average wage' in their country, most of them are below it. This isn't a fluke — it's a feature of skewed distributions like income, where a few huge values pull the mean up but most observations sit lower.
items.prompt: What's the difference that matters here?

options.text: There is no difference — these terms are interchangeable
Mean (arithmetic average) is pulled by extreme values; median (50th percentile) splits the population in half; for income distributions, the mean is well above the median because of high earners

items.reveal:
Three common 'averages':
- Mean: sum of values divided by count. Sensitive to extreme values.
- Median: the middle value when sorted. Robust to extremes.
- Mode: the most common value. Useful for categorical data.

For a symmetric distribution (like adult height), mean ≈ median ≈ mode. The 'typical' person is well-described by any of them.

For skewed distributions:
- Right-skewed (income, wealth, city size): mean > median > mode. A few huge values pull the mean up.
- Left-skewed (test scores with a ceiling): mean < median.

US household income (2022): mean ~115,000 USD, median ~75,000. The 'average household' as measured by mean is income that 60% of households fall below.

Dangers of using mean carelessly: 'the average net worth in this room is 100 million USD' (because Elon Musk just walked in). For policy and individual planning, median is often more informative.

The terms have legal force: a statement that 'most people earn the average wage' is misleading for income, even if it would be roughly true for height.
items.why: 'Average' has many meanings, and in skewed distributions they diverge dramatically. Almost every report on income, wealth or wait times that uses the word 'average' should be parsed carefully.
